title: Detection Strategy for Weaken Encryption on Network Devices
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Weaken Encryption on Network Devices
summary: This detection strategy covers Weaken Encryption (T1600) on network devices such as routers, switches and firewalls. An adversary who already holds privileged access to a device can lower or disable the cryptography used by management protocols or by a virtual private network tunnel, which allows traffic that should be protected to be read or altered in transit. The telemetry that makes the change visible is device configuration change logging, accounting records for privileged management sessions, and configuration backup comparisons. The detection most often fails because many organisations never ship network device logs to their central platform, and because the same commands appear in legitimate maintenance work.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for changes that make encryption weaker on network devices. Network devices are the routers and switches that move your traffic. The rule watches for commands that turn encryption off or move it to an older and weaker setting.
beginner.whyItMatters: When encryption gets weaker, an attacker can read traffic that should be secret. The change often looks like normal maintenance, so nobody questions it. If you see the change early, you can stop the attacker before data is stolen. You also keep a clean record for the later investigation. A weak setting can stay on a device for months without anyone asking why.
howItWorks: The network device writes a log line each time an administrator changes its configuration.
Your central log platform collects those lines from every router, switch and firewall you own.
The rule looks for key words about encryption, such as a cipher list or a tunnel setting.
It compares the new value with the approved baseline for that device model and software version.
When the setting moves to a weaker value, the rule raises an alert and names the account.
An analyst then checks the change ticket to decide whether the change was approved.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman who checks the locks on every door of a building. A weak lock still looks like a lock, so the watchman must test it, not just look at it. This detection is that test. It does not ask whether a door exists. It asks whether the door is still strong enough to keep people out.
takeaways: A weak encryption setting is a quiet change, not a loud attack.
You need device logs shipped to one place, or you cannot see this at all.
Always compare the change with an approved baseline before you alert.

objectives: Explain how weakening encryption on a network device helps an adversary read protected traffic
Identify the device logs and accounting records that record a privileged configuration change
Build a baseline of approved cipher, key exchange and tunnel settings for each device model
Write a rule that compares a configuration change against that baseline and the change calendar
Triage alerts by checking the account, the time, the source address and the change ticket
Describe which devices and traffic types are lost when the rule is scoped down for noise
dataSources: Network device configuration change logs forwarded over syslog from routers, switches and firewalls
Command history and TACACS plus or RADIUS accounting records for privileged device management sessions
Authentication records for device management interfaces such as SSH and HTTPS administration sessions
Scheduled configuration backup files compared between versions to reveal changed cipher and tunnel settings
logic: The pattern is a configuration change that lowers the strength of encryption, written to device change logging shortly after a privileged login. The fields that must be correlated are the device identity, the administrator account, the configuration line or command that changed, and the time of the session. The benign case is a scheduled maintenance window with an approved change ticket, a known administrator account and a matching baseline update. The malicious case is an out of hours change made by an account with no change ticket, often followed by a login from an unusual source address or by a new tunnel peer.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Network Device Encryption Setting Weakened
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: configuration_change
#     config_command: '*no crypto*'
#   selection_cipher:
#     config_command: '*cipher*'
#   filter_maintenance:
#     change_ticket: approved
#   condition: (selection or selection_cipher) and not filter_maintenance
# level: high
falsePositives: Planned firmware upgrades that reset the cipher list to a vendor default before the new policy is applied
An on call engineer disabling tunnel encryption while troubleshooting a site to site link during an outage
Legacy devices that only support older cipher suites and are re-enabled during failover
Lab or test devices that are outside the production baseline and are reconfigured freely
tuningNotes: First scope the rule to devices that carry regulated or sensitive traffic, and filter out maintenance windows that are published in your change calendar. Baseline the normal cipher, key exchange and tunnel settings for each device model, so the rule compares a change with that device's own history rather than one global value. Exclude lab ranges and any device that only supports legacy cryptography. Narrowing this way removes most of the noise, but you lose sight of production devices that are quietly reconfigured outside a window, so keep a lower severity version of the same rule running across all devices.
